The network of the instruments

Every relationship recorded between the instruments this site names, drawn as a network: the instruments are the points and the recorded relationships are the lines, and nothing else is. No line is inferred, and none is drawn from a shared provision, claim or source. The list with the network is the record; the network is its picture. A relationship absent here has not been recorded, which is not a finding that it does not exist.

In tension with2

Cloud and AI Development Act Proposed: in tension with Data Act

The Data Act mandates open interoperability and the elimination of lock-in; the sovereignty requirements of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act push toward highly secure, localised environments. The two pull in opposite directions.

Characterisation requires verification. Migrated to the v2 shape on 15 Nov 2026 (V2C-12), on the author's decision. Read that day in the texts retrieved from the Publications Office's Cellar by CELEX, not at the EUR-Lex URLs. (COM(2026) 502 final: the body and memorandum from the Council transmission ST 10104/26 and, for the Annexes, which that transmission does not hold, Cellar's manifestation of 52026PC0502; CELEX 32023R2854.) The kind and the summary are the author's critique (see the claim) and are not changed. What is carried: Annex II of the proposal makes recognition at Union assurance levels 1-4 depend on criteria including infrastructure and assets located in the Union (point 1.1(b), subject to the public sector body requiring otherwise) and customer data remaining exclusively within the Union (points 1.1(c), 2.1(c), 3.1(c), 4.1(c)), with Union-citizen personnel at levels 3-4 and no third-country control: "localised" is read. The Data Act mandates switching and portability (Art. 23; Art. 25(2): a 30-day transitional period, a notice period of at most two months, an exhaustive specification of exportable data); its interoperability rules are in Chapter VIII (Arts 33-36), which was not read beyond what is cited. WHAT THE ONE PRIMARY TEXT THAT SPEAKS TO THE RELATIONSHIP SAYS, IN FULL, AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF "CONFLICT": the memorandum states that "The proposal is consistent with the rules on switching between data processing services introduced by the Data Act", that the Data Act "opens the path towards a possible reduction of dependencies on non-EU providers but does not build the road towards a more sovereign and trusted EU cloud computing sector", that "Its cloud switching and interoperability provisions, however, make it possible for users to embrace European cloud computing services more strongly", and that "The Data Act is thus an enabler for the proposal"; its section 1.5.3 says the proposal "builds on and complements" provisions of the Data Act. Whether a tension in effect exists (for example between the localisation criteria and a customer's freedom to switch to a provider outside the Union) is an analytical question no text read asserts or refutes. A proposal's text is the Commission's, not what the co-legislators may adopt. No corrigendum to any of these acts was looked up.

Carried byData Act Art. 25
What the brief argues
  • InterpretationSovereignty and interoperability pull in opposite directions: the Data Act was designed to mandate open interoperability and eliminate lock-in, while the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act's sovereignty requirements push toward highly secure, localised environments.
Sources
  • Council of the European UnionTier 2 · regulatorCOM(2026) 502 final, explanatory memorandum, "Consistency with existing policy provisions in the policy area"; Art. 16 (Union cloud computing sovereignty framework; its criteria are in Annex II, which this transmission does not reproduce)
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 23; Art. 25(2)
  • The European Legal Framework for the Digital World (this brief)Unverified · the brief itselfPart X

DSA In tension with GDPR

Content moderation, notice and action and advertising transparency all involve processing personal data. The DSA requires each advertisement to be explained in real time, including its main targeting parameters, while the GDPR requires information when the data are obtained and their minimisation. EDPB guidance mediates the conflict but does not dissolve it.

Carried byDSA Art. 16
What the brief argues
  • InterpretationThe DSA–GDPR interface is unresolved: the DSA tells platforms to be transparent while the GDPR tells them to minimise, and EDPB guidance mediates the conflict without dissolving it.
Sources
  • European Data Protection BoardTier 2 · regulatorGuidelines 3/2025 v2, ¶¶7–11; section 2.2 (Arts 16, 17, 20 and 23 DSA); ¶¶53–58 and 79–80 (Art. 26 DSA); ¶6 excludes Art. 40

Overlaps with3

AI Act Overlaps with GDPR

Both instruments reach the same conduct.

GDPR Art. 22 has governed solely-automated decision-making since 2018, including systems the AI Act classifies as minimal risk. The AI Act arrived into a field the GDPR already occupied.

Carried byGDPR Art. 22AI Act Art. 6
What the brief argues
  • Primary lawGDPR Article 22 is the pre-existing European law of automated decision-making: it did not wait for the AI Act and applies to systems the AI Act classifies as minimal risk.
  • InterpretationThe AI Act is one instrument in a system that already regulated most of its subject matter: automated decision-making by GDPR Art. 22 since 2018, algorithmic recommender risk by DSA Arts. 34–35, product liability by the revised PLD — while the proposed AI Liability Directive was abandoned, leaving a gap in the fault-based route.
Sources
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 22(1); Art. 99(2) (applies from 25 May 2018)
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 6 (classification rules for high-risk AI systems)

Recorded as at 27 October 2026

AI Act Overlaps with GDPR

Both instruments reach the same conduct.

GDPR Art. 35 DPIAs, DSA Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and AI Act Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment are three overlapping assessment duties that regulators themselves acknowledge are duplicated.

Characterisation requires verification. Migrated to the v2 shape on 15 Nov 2026 (V2C-12), on the author's decision. Read that day in the texts retrieved from the Publications Office's Cellar by CELEX, not at the EUR-Lex URLs. (CELEX 32024R1689, 32016R0679, 32022R2065.) AI Act Art. 27(4): where an obligation of Art. 27 is already met through the data protection impact assessment under GDPR Art. 35, the fundamental rights impact assessment "shall complement" it; GDPR Art. 35(1) and AI Act Art. 27(1) set out the two duties (different addressees: controllers; certain deployers of high-risk AI systems). DSA Art. 34(1) is a third assessment duty, of providers of very large online platforms and search engines, whose scope includes the protection of personal data (point (b)); no text read links it to Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 AI Act. WHAT NO TEXT READ CARRIES: that "regulators themselves acknowledge" the three duties are duplicated (the one acknowledgement found, Art. 27(4), is the legislator's, concerns two of the three, and says "complement"), and that an organisation running all three duplicates work. Both stay what a separate claim says they are: not sourced. No corrigendum to any of these acts was looked up.

Carried byGDPR Art. 35DSA Art. 34AI Act Art. 27
What the brief argues
  • InterpretationGDPR Art. 35 DPIAs, DSA Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and AI Act Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment are three overlapping assessment duties; an organisation running all three separately duplicates work regulators themselves acknowledge is duplicated.
Sources
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 27(1) and (4)
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 35(1)
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 34(1), point (b)

Recorded as at 15 November 2026

Carves out from1

TEU Carves out from AI Act

Article 4(2) TEU reserves national security to the Member States, and the AI Act does not apply to AI systems placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes (Art. 2(3)). The brief argues this is the structural source of the asymmetry between constraint on corporate and on state power.

Carried byTEU Art. 4(2)AI Act Art. 2(3)
What the brief argues
  • Primary lawArticle 4(2) TEU reserves national security to the Member States: it remains the sole responsibility of each Member State.
  • InterpretationThis body of law restrains corporate power far more effectively than it restrains state power, and on the record available the enforcement asymmetry between corporate and state addressees is hard to dispute.
Sources
  • Publications Office of the European Union (Cellar)Tier 1 · primary lawArt. 4(2), third sentence
  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 2(3), second subparagraph; recital (24)
  • The European Legal Framework for the Digital World (this brief)Unverified · the brief itselfPart XI

Complements5

AI Act Complements Revised PLD

The AI Act is product-safety legislation; the revised Product Liability Directive brings software and AI within strict product liability. The proposed AI Liability Directive, which would have covered the fault-based route, was abandoned.

What the brief argues
  • Official sourceThe proposed AI Liability Directive was abandoned, leaving a gap in the fault-based liability route.
  • Primary lawThe revised Product Liability Directive brings software and AI within strict product liability, applying to products placed on the market or put into service from 9 December 2026.

  • EUR-LexTier 1 · primary lawArt. 4 point (1) ('product' … includes … software); recital 13 (software, including AI systems)

Data Omnibus Proposed: amends GDPR

PROPOSED amendment only. The Digital Omnibus proposes changes to the personal-data definition, a new Art. 41a, relocation of cookie consent to Art. 88a and a new Art. 88c. None is law.

What the brief argues
  • Primary lawThe Commission's four principal proposed GDPR reforms were: an entity-relative test for personal data in Art. 4(1); a new Art. 41a empowering the Commission to set, by implementing acts, the means and criteria for determining when pseudonymised data ceases to be personal; relocation of cookie consent into a new Art. 88a; and a new Art. 88c providing an explicit legitimate-interest basis for AI model training. None is law.
Sources
  • European CommissionTier 1 · legislative proposalArt. 3 (amendments to Regulation (EU) 2016/679): point 1(a) (Art. 4(1), added sentences); point 10 (new Art. 41a); point 15 (new Arts 88a and 88c)

NIS2 Enables Cyber Solidarity Act

The other instrument's provisions operate through definitions, bodies, means or populations this instrument establishes, and say so. Recorded only on an express reference in the DEPENDENT instrument's text; the locator is in that text. Added 27 Oct 2026.

The Cyber Solidarity Act defines CSIRTs, entities, the entities of sectors of high criticality and other critical sectors, risk, incident, significant and large-scale cybersecurity incidents and managed security service providers by reference to NIS2.

How to read this view

A line is a record. Each line is one of the relationships recorded in the instruments dataset, which Datasets shows as written, with its type, its sources and, where the record has them, the provisions and the claims that carry it. Two relationships between the same two instruments are two lines. An arrow is drawn only where the record gives a direction; a mutual relationship has none.

Proposed is not the law. Where the act that would state a relationship is not adopted, the relationship is read “Proposed: …” and drawn faint and thin. That is derived from the instruments’ recorded status each time the page loads, never stored, as it is on every other page of this site.

Not every instrument is analysed. The site covers some instruments, maps others for their links, and names others it watches or deliberately excludes; each point says which, by its fill and outline as well as in words.

The picture is computed, not curated. The positions come from a fixed calculation over the records — related instruments drawn together — with no randomness, so the same records give the same network. Nearness on the screen is not a legal statement.
